title: A Name Above the Door
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The old sign came down in two pieces.

One half still said RESTRICTED ACCESS. The other had been painted over so many times that the original letters showed through in the rain.

Danse stood beneath the empty brackets with a screwdriver in his hand.

"I should have changed it months ago," he said.

"You changed the door first," I answered.

He looked toward the entrance.

The workshop was open. Not unguarded, not careless, but designed for the people who used it. Edda could reach the bell. Ash could close the private workroom from inside. Renn and Aster had signed the repair schedule with their actual hours. The emergency exit opened without waiting for a former soldier to approve it.

The sign was the last thing that still spoke in the old voice.

Tamsin arrived carrying a fresh board.

"What are we calling it?" she asked.

Danse looked at me.

I raised an eyebrow.

"It's your workshop."

He looked surprised.

It had taken him a long time to understand that choosing a name did not require someone else to grant him a title.

He looked at the board.

"Brasswatch Open Workshop," he said.

Tamsin smiled.

"Good. I can fit that."

She painted the letters in a deep blue that matched the safe-route signs. Beneath them she added smaller words, approved by the people who worked there:

REPAIRS • TRAINING • SHELTER BY CHOICE.

Danse read the line.

"Should it say no rank required?"

Renn, standing nearby, laughed.

"Only if you promise not to invent a new one."

Danse smiled.

"No ranks."

We raised the sign together.

It wasn't a ceremony. Tamsin held the ladder, Renn guided the brackets, and I passed up the screws. Danse did the final tightening, then climbed down and stepped back.

The board was level.

The door was open.

For a moment none of us spoke.

Then Ash came out of the private room and looked at the sign.

"Better," they said.

Danse nodded.

"Thank you."

Ash did not hug him, forgive him, or tell him he'd become a different person. They went back inside to finish their work.

He let them.

That mattered.

The opening day drew a few people who had avoided the workshop before. One brought a broken kettle. Another asked whether there was a safe place to repair a wheeled cart. A young traveler wanted to learn how to read a pressure gauge.

Renn ran the beginner's lesson. Danse watched for a while, then stepped away when it became clear they didn't need him hovering.

I caught his expression.

"Hard?" I asked.

"Very."

"You're doing well."

"An alarming statement."

I laughed.

The young traveler's first lesson did not go as planned.

Renn had set out a pressure gauge, two small hoses and a tray for collecting water. The student, Ilya's cousin Niko, followed every instruction carefully until the second fitting refused to catch. Their hands began to shake.

"I'm sorry," Niko said.

"What for?" Renn asked.

"I've wasted the lesson."

Danse stood a few steps away, very still.

I could see the sentence he'd been trained to say years ago: *You were given clear instructions.* He had no intention of using it, but the struggle to find different words showed in his face.

Renn took the gauge from Niko.

"The fitting is worn," they said. "I should have checked it before the lesson."

Niko looked surprised.

"It isn't my fault?"

"It might have been a mistake even if it were," Renn said. "That would be part of learning."

Danse stepped closer.

"Would you like to see how we test whether a fitting is safe to reuse?"

Niko nodded.

"All right. We will start there."

He didn't take the tools and do the repair himself. He showed the student where the thread had flattened, then handed the piece back and waited while Niko compared it with the new fitting.

The student found the difference.

"That's why it won't catch."

"Correct," Danse said.

The word held no threat.

I looked toward the open exit, where the safe-route sign had been set at a height Edda could read. People were working at their own benches, answering questions, arguing about measurements, earning their wages. A workshop rather than a barracks.

Later Niko asked whether a lesson could be scheduled for next week.

Renn checked the calendar.

"We can. I'll have a better fitting ready."

Danse smiled.

I found him afterward washing the used tools.

"You looked frightened when Niko apologized," I said.

"I was remembering what happened to people who made mistakes under my command."

He shut off the water.

"I can't change those moments."

"No."

"I can make sure this room doesn't repeat them."

I put the dry cloth beside him.

"That sounds like a good reason to keep the door open."

He looked at me with a small, tired tenderness.

"One of several," he said.

At noon, Toph arrived to inspect the new support beam. She tapped the stone, listened for the familiar movement, and declared the repair satisfactory under the conditions of the test.

Danse checked the written measurement.

It matched.

"Almost competent," Toph said.

He smiled.

"High praise."

She grinned and left before he could thank her.

The afternoon moved on. A lantern flickered at the edge of the yard, and someone asked Pip to replace the wick. Mara delivered bread for the volunteers. The generator ran within its safe load.

Nothing dramatic happened.

I thought Danse might be disappointed.

Instead he looked almost peaceful.

After closing, we sat on the back steps with two cups of tea.

He stared at the new sign.

"I spent years believing I knew who I was because I wore armor," he said.

"And now?"

"Now I know what I want to do when I take it off."

I looked at him.

"Repair things?"

"Yes. Teach what I know. Learn what I don't. Make room for people who need shelter without demanding their names as payment."

I felt warmth move through my chest.

"That sounds like a life."

He looked toward me.

"Would you like to be part of it?"

"I already am."

He smiled.

"And you have other lives, other people you love. I know we agreed to that. I know you're ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. I don't want to ask you to abandon any of it."

"Then what are you asking?"

"For the chance to keep choosing this with you. The ordinary days. The difficult talks. The mistakes we correct."

I took his hand.

"Yes."

He looked almost relieved enough to laugh.

"That's a lot of responsibility."

"Good thing you're capable of writing a checklist."

He laughed.

I kissed him, slow and warm. His hand rested against the back of my neck, gentle and sure. We stayed close until the light above the workshop door came on and the yard grew quiet.

Later, inside, the rest of the evening belonged to us. No rank, no audience, no need to make the tenderness visible to anyone else.

In the morning, Danse opened the workshop at the posted hour.

Renn was already there with a student who wanted to learn how to replace a worn hinge. The kettle from yesterday had been repaired and was ready to collect. The emergency exit was clear.

Danse put on his work gloves.

"Morning," he said.

"Morning," Renn answered.

They handed him the inspection sheet.

He read it, made one correction, and gave it back.

Then he stepped aside so the student could begin.

Outside, the sign caught the early light.

Brasswatch Open Workshop.

A name he'd chosen.

A door anyone could ask to enter.

A place he could leave at the end of the day and still choose to return.
